safe_ratio <- function(numerator, denominator) {
  if_else(!is.na(denominator) & denominator > 0, numerator / denominator, NA_real_)
}

winsorise_upper <- function(x, p = 0.99) {
  cap <- quantile(x, probs = p, na.rm = TRUE)
  pmin(x, cap)
}

1 Assignment purpose and analytical design

This report addresses the ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 requirement: use visual analytics for data discovery on a motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset. The analytical target is not only to describe the portfolio, but to identify where profitability and volatility differ across policy, customer, vehicle, and exposure characteristics.

The report uses the following logic:

  1. Data audit and preparation: verify row structure, missingness, duplicates, variable types, and construct actuarial performance metrics.
  2. Univariate visual analytics: examine the standalone distributions of premium, claims, incurred losses, exposure, loss ratio, and portfolio composition.
  3. Bivariate visual analytics: test how profitability and volatility differ by product, payment, claims-history, geography, vehicle, and policy-status segments.
  4. Statistical validation: support visual patterns with non-parametric tests and frequency modelling.
  5. Business interpretation: translate visual evidence into underwriting, pricing, and portfolio-management implications.

1.1 Rubric alignment and deliverable logic

The technical report is written to support the Executive Summary rather than repeat it. The Executive Summary presents the decision story; this report documents the reproducible analytical evidence behind that story. The following table maps the report design to the assignment assessment logic.

Assessment area How this report addresses it
Data wrangling Imports the raw semicolon-delimited portfolio file, reconciles the data dictionary, audits row structure, checks duplicates and missingness, converts categorical fields, and engineers exposure-adjusted performance metrics.
Visual analysis Uses univariate and bivariate visual analytics to examine premium adequacy, claim frequency, severity, loss-ratio skewness, product effects, customer/vehicle/geography effects, and interaction effects.
Visual communication Uses chart types selected for the structure of each question: bar charts for segment comparison, histograms for skewness, raincloud and ridgeline plots for distribution shape, funnel plots for exposure-adjusted outliers, and heatmaps for interactions.
Reproducibility Shows the full R workflow: package loading, data import, cleaning, metric construction, plotting, summary tables, and statistical validation.
Additional visual methods Adds raincloud plots, ridgeline plots, funnel-plot logic, and interaction heatmaps beyond simple descriptive charts.

The methods are selected from the R for Visual Analytics materials only when they fit the data structure. Because insurance losses are highly right-skewed and zero-inflated, the report avoids relying only on means. It uses weighted portfolio loss ratios, exposure-adjusted claim frequency, winsorised distributions, raincloud plots, ridgeline plots, heatmaps, and model-supported visual diagnostics.

dictionary_raw |>
  select(variables, description, group) |>
  filter(!is.na(variables)) |>
  gt::gt()
variables description group
insured_id Unique identifier assigned to each policy number. Policy and insured characteristics
year Calendar year Policy and insured characteristics
policy_type Categorical variable describing the main coverage structure of the motor insurance policy. The original detailed combinations have been grouped into broader, actuarially meaningful categories. Policy and insured characteristics
policy_status Indicates whether the policy was active (A) or cancelled (C) at the time of analysis. Policy and insured characteristics
business_type Classification of the policy according to its business origin. Policy and insured characteristics
payment_frequency Indicates the policy’s billing frequency: Policy and insured characteristics
bonus_score Indicator of the policyholder’s past claims experience: Policy and insured characteristics
driver_age Age of the main driver associated with the policy, measured in years. Driver and vehicle characteristics
vehicle_age Age of the insured vehicle, also measured in years. Driver and vehicle characteristics
age_driving_licence Year in which the insured obtained the driving licence. Driver and vehicle characteristics
fuel_type Indicates the vehicle’s fuel type. In this dataset, only two categories are kept: Driver and vehicle characteristics
vehicle_value Declared insured value of the vehicle. Some entries are missing Driver and vehicle characteristics
seats Number of seats available in the insured vehicle. Driver and vehicle characteristics
power_to_weight_ratio Approximate weight-to-power ratio of the vehicle (kg per horsepower), used as a proxy for performance characteristics. Driver and vehicle characteristics
vehicle_brand Brand of the insured vehicle as reported in the policy data. Driver and vehicle characteristics
municipality_type Geographic classification of the policyholder’s municipality: Driver and vehicle characteristics
circulation_area Indicates the predominant circulation environment of the vehicle: Driver and vehicle characteristics
total_premium Total premium of the policy, calculated as the sum of all individual coverage premiums. Premiums
liability_premium Premium charged for third-party liability coverage. Premiums
property_damage_premium Premium corresponding to property damage coverage. Premiums
theft_premium Premium associated with theft coverage. Premiums
fire_premium Premium for fire coverage. Premiums
glass_premium Premium for glass coverage. Premiums
legal_protection_premium Premium for legal protection coverage. Premiums
occupants_premium Premium for personal-injury coverage of vehicle occupants. Premiums
total_claims Indicates the total number of claims reported for the policy during the exposure period. Typical values range from 0 (no claims) to several claims per contract. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_claims Total number of liability claims reported under the policy. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_property_claims Number of liability claims related to material or property damage. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_injury_claims Number of liability claims involving bodily injury. Exposure, claims and incurred
property_claims Count of property damage claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
theft_claims Number of theft-related claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
fire_claims Count of fire-related claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
glass_claims Number of glass-related claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
legal_protection_claims Number of legal protection claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
occupants_claims Number of claims under this coverage. Exposure, claims and incurred
total_incurred Represents the total incurred cost of claims for the policy, including paid amounts and outstanding reserves. Values are typically zero for policies without losses and positive when claims exist. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_incurred Total incurred cost (paid + reserved) for all liability claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_property_incurred Total incurred cost for liability claims involving material or property damage. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_injury_incurred Total incurred cost for liability claims involving bodily injury. Exposure, claims and incurred
property_incurred Total incurred cost for property damage claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
theft_incurred Total incurred cost for theft claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
fire_incurred Total incurred cost for fire claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
glass_incurred Total incurred cost for glass claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
legal_protection_incurred Total incurred cost for legal protection claims. Exposure, claims and incurred
occupants_incurred Total incurred cost under this coverage. Exposure, claims and incurred
total_exposure Represents the effective time-on-risk for each policy, expressed in policy years. Values range from 0 to 1 for partial-year exposure, and may exceed 1 if the contract covers more than one year. Exposure, claims and incurred
liability_exposure Amount of exposure associated with liability coverage. Exposure, claims and incurred

The CSV is semicolon-delimited. The data dictionary is used to verify variable meanings before metric engineering. The unit of observation is a policy-year record: the same insured_id may appear across multiple years.

Code 
dictionary_variables <- dictionary_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(variables)) |>
  pull(variables) |>
  janitor::make_clean_names()

column_check <- tibble(
  variable = union(names(portfolio_raw), dictionary_variables)
) |>
  mutate(
    in_dataset = variable %in% names(portfolio_raw),
    in_dictionary = variable %in% dictionary_variables
  )

column_check |>
  filter(!in_dataset | !in_dictionary) |>
  gt::gt()
variable in_dataset in_dictionary

A clean analysis should explicitly check whether dataset columns match the variable dictionary. Any mismatch would undermine reproducibility and interpretation.

Only a small number of variables contain missing values. They are not dropped wholesale because insurance missingness may itself be informative. For visual analytics, missing categories are explicitly retained as "Unknown" where relevant.

3.2 Metric engineering

Code 
portfolio <- portfolio_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency,
        bonus_score, fuel_type, vehicle_brand, municipality_type, circulation_area),
      ~fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.x), level = "Unknown")
    ),
    claim_flag = total_claims > 0,
    loss_ratio = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_premium),
    profit = total_premium - total_incurred,
    profit_margin = safe_ratio(total_premium - total_incurred, total_premium),
    claim_frequency = safe_ratio(total_claims, total_exposure),
    premium_rate = safe_ratio(total_premium, total_exposure),
    incurred_rate = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_exposure),
    claim_severity = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_claims),
    log_total_premium = log1p(total_premium),
    log_total_incurred = log1p(total_incurred),
    loss_ratio_w99 = winsorise_upper(loss_ratio, 0.99),
    incurred_w99 = winsorise_upper(total_incurred, 0.99),
    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf),
      labels = c("≤25", "26–35", "36–45", "46–55", "56–65", "66+")
    ),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 3, 7, 12, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("≤3", "4–7", "8–12", "13–20", "21+")
    ),
    vehicle_value_band = ntile(vehicle_value, 5),
    vehicle_value_band = factor(
      vehicle_value_band,
      levels = 1:5,
      labels = c("Lowest value", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Highest value")
    )
  )

The key profitability measure is the portfolio loss ratio:

[ = ]

A value below 1 indicates underwriting profit before expenses; a value above 1 indicates that incurred claims exceed premium. For segment comparison, this report prioritises portfolio-level weighted loss ratio (sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium)) over simple average policy-level loss ratio, because large-premium policies should carry proportionate weight in portfolio profitability.

Volatility is represented by:

  • dispersion of policy-level loss ratio;
  • extreme incurred losses;
  • claim frequency per exposure year;
  • coefficient of variation of incurred cost;
  • outlier-sensitive segment loss ratios.
Code 
portfolio |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    total_exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    portfolio_loss_ratio = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_premium_rate = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_claim_severity = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(total_exposure, total_premium, total_incurred, total_claims,
             portfolio_loss_ratio, claim_frequency, avg_premium_rate, avg_claim_severity),
           ~round(.x, 3))
  ) |>
  gt::gt()

4 Univariate visual analytics

4.1 Portfolio growth and exposure composition

Code 
annual_summary <- portfolio |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    policies = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    portfolio_loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    premium_rate = premium / exposure,
    avg_severity = incurred / claims,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

annual_summary |>
  mutate(
    portfolio_loss_ratio = percent(portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1),
    claim_frequency = number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.001),
    premium_rate = dollar(premium_rate, prefix = "€", accuracy = 1),
    avg_severity = dollar(avg_severity, prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()

Code 
p_annual_volume <- annual_summary |>
  pivot_longer(c(premium, incurred), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = value, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("premium" = my_light, "incurred" = my_blue)) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium and incurred losses both increased with portfolio growth",
    x = NULL, y = "Amount", fill = NULL
  )

p_annual_lr <- annual_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = portfolio_loss_ratio)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = my_blue) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = my_blue) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(annual_summary$year))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Portfolio loss ratio rose over time",
    x = NULL, y = "Portfolio loss ratio"
  )

p_annual_volume + p_annual_lr

The annual summary is essential because the assignment asks for discovery of profitability and volatility. The portfolio is not static: exposure, premium, incurred losses, and claim frequency all change over time.

4.2 Distribution of premium, incurred losses, and loss ratio

Code 
p_premium <- portfolio |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium distribution is right-skewed",
    x = "Total premium", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_incurred <- portfolio |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log1p(total_incurred))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Incurred loss is zero-heavy and extreme-tailed",
    x = "log(1 + total incurred)", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_lr <- portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio_w99)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Winsorised loss ratio reveals core risk distribution",
    x = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_premium + p_incurred + p_lr

The incurred-loss distribution is structurally different from the premium distribution. Premium is continuous and right-skewed, whereas incurred loss has many zero values and a heavy tail. This supports the use of robust visualisations and exposure-weighted metrics rather than raw averages alone.

4.3 Claim count distribution

Code 
portfolio |>
  count(total_claims) |>
  mutate(
    claim_count_label = if_else(total_claims >= 5, "5+", as.character(total_claims))
  ) |>
  group_by(claim_count_label) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    claim_count_label = factor(claim_count_label, levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5+")),
    pct = n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_count_label, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_blue, colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Most policy-years have no claim, so claim occurrence must be modelled separately",
    x = "Total claims in policy-year", y = "Share of policy-years"
  )

This confirms a typical insurance portfolio pattern: most policies do not claim, while a minority drives incurred losses. That is why frequency and severity should be separated analytically.

4.4 Product composition

Code 
policy_composition <- portfolio |>
  group_by(policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    policies = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    policy_share = policies / sum(policies),
    exposure_share = exposure / sum(exposure),
    premium_share = premium / sum(premium),
    incurred_share = incurred / sum(incurred)
  )

policy_composition |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(policy_share, exposure_share, premium_share, incurred_share),
    names_to = "basis", values_to = "share"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    basis = recode(
      basis,
      policy_share = "Policy count",
      exposure_share = "Exposure",
      premium_share = "Premium",
      incurred_share = "Incurred"
    ),
    policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, share, .fun = max)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = share, fill = basis)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D8E6F3", "#A9C7E8", "#6B9FD3", "#2F6DAE")) +
  labs(
    title = "Product mix is not the same as premium and incurred-loss mix",
    x = "Policy type", y = "Share of portfolio", fill = NULL
  )

Portfolio management should distinguish between count share, exposure share, premium share, and incurred share. A product with modest policy count can still dominate premium or loss contribution if coverage is broader or riskier.

4.5 Ridgeline plot of premium rate by product

Code 
portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(premium_rate), is.finite(premium_rate)) |>
  mutate(premium_rate_w99 = winsorise_upper(premium_rate, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = premium_rate_w99, y = fct_reorder(policy_type, premium_rate_w99, .fun = median))) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.4,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.3),
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline plot shows premium-rate separation across policy types",
    x = "Premium per exposure year, capped at 99th percentile",
    y = NULL
  )

This method is taken from the R4VA distribution chapter. It is suitable here because policy_type has multiple ordered groups and premium_rate is a continuous metric.

4.6 Raincloud plot of loss ratio by product

Code 
portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w99), is.finite(loss_ratio_w99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio_w99, .fun = median), y = loss_ratio_w99)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.18,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.35)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.16, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white", colour = my_dark) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.12,
    binwidth = 0.05,
    dotsize = 0.6,
    colour = my_blue
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud plot combines density, boxplot, and individual concentration",
    x = NULL, y = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile"
  )

The raincloud plot is stronger than a standard boxplot for this task because it exposes distribution shape and concentration while retaining median and IQR information. This directly supports the visual-discovery requirement.

4.7 Distribution-shape add-on for adverse-experience policies

The Executive Summary includes a distribution-shape add-on because the portfolio is zero-heavy: most policy-year records have no claims, while a small tail of adverse-experience policies drives volatility. This technical view deliberately filters to positive loss-ratio records and caps the displayed tail at the 95th percentile. The purpose is not to hide severe losses; the purpose is to make the shape among adverse records readable after the report has already established the scale of zero-claim dominance.

Code 
positive_loss <- portfolio |>
  filter(
    !is.na(loss_ratio),
    is.finite(loss_ratio),
    loss_ratio > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(loss_ratio_positive_w95 = winsorise_upper(loss_ratio, 0.95))

p_positive_raincloud <- positive_loss |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio_positive_w95, .fun = median),
    y = loss_ratio_positive_w95
  )) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.6,
    justification = -0.16,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.40)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.14, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white", colour = my_dark) +
  ggdist::stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.08,
    binwidth = 0.04,
    dotsize = 0.45,
    colour = my_blue
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Positive-loss distribution by product",
    subtitle = "Zero-claim records excluded; loss ratio capped at 95th percentile for readability",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Positive loss ratio, capped"
  )

p_positive_ridgeline <- positive_loss |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = loss_ratio_positive_w95,
    y = fct_reorder(payment_frequency, loss_ratio_positive_w95, .fun = median)
  )) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.0,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.35),
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  ggridges::theme_ridges() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Positive-loss density by payment frequency",
    subtitle = "Compares adverse-experience distributions without the zero-claim mass",
    x = "Positive loss ratio, capped",
    y = NULL
  )

p_positive_raincloud + p_positive_ridgeline

The raincloud plot is appropriate because it combines distribution density, boxplot summary, and observation concentration in one view. The ridgeline plot is appropriate because it compares distribution shape across multiple ordered groups without forcing the reader to inspect separate charts. Together, these methods justify the executive conclusion that simple averages are unstable for this portfolio.

5 Bivariate visual analytics

5.1 Segment-performance function

Code 
segment_summary <- function(data, segment_var) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ segment_var }}) |>
    summarise(
      policies = n(),
      exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
      incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
      portfolio_loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
      claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
      premium_rate = premium / exposure,
      avg_severity = incurred / claims,
      mean_policy_loss_ratio = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_policy_loss_ratio = sd(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
      cv_incurred = sd(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(portfolio_loss_ratio))
}

For profitability, portfolio_loss_ratio is the primary measure. For volatility, this report uses claim frequency, average severity, policy-level loss-ratio dispersion, and incurred-loss coefficient of variation.

5.8 Funnel plot for exposure-adjusted brand screening

The Executive Summary includes a funnel plot because raw segment rankings can overreact to small-volume groups. In insurance portfolios, a vehicle brand with limited exposure can show an extreme claim frequency simply because the denominator is small. A funnel plot is therefore more defensible than a simple sorted bar chart when the analytical question is whether a segment is unusually high after accounting for exposure volume.

The funnel uses claim frequency as the outcome and exposure years as the denominator. The centre line is the overall portfolio claim frequency. The approximate 95% band widens at low exposure and narrows at high exposure, reflecting the higher random variation expected in small segments.

Code 
brand_funnel <- portfolio |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= quantile(exposure, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = fct_lump_n(vehicle_brand, n = 25, w = exposure)) |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(exposure),
    claims = sum(claims),
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(vehicle_brand != "Other")

overall_rate <- sum(portfolio$total_claims, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(portfolio$total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE)

funnel_curve <- tibble(
  exposure = seq(min(brand_funnel$exposure), max(brand_funnel$exposure), length.out = 200),
  expected = overall_rate,
  upper_95 = overall_rate + 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate / exposure),
  lower_95 = pmax(overall_rate - 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate / exposure), 0)
)

flagged_brand <- brand_funnel |>
  mutate(distance = abs(claim_frequency - overall_rate)) |>
  slice_max(distance, n = 6, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = funnel_curve,
    aes(x = exposure, ymin = lower_95, ymax = upper_95),
    fill = "#D9E8F6",
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = funnel_curve,
    aes(x = exposure, y = expected),
    colour = my_blue,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = brand_funnel,
    aes(x = exposure, y = claim_frequency),
    colour = my_teal,
    size = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = flagged_brand,
    aes(x = exposure, y = claim_frequency, label = vehicle_brand),
    size = 3,
    vjust = -0.7,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Funnel plot: claim frequency by vehicle brand",
    subtitle = "Approximate 95% expected range after accounting for exposure size",
    x = "Exposure years",
    y = "Claims per exposure year"
  )

The funnel plot adds value because it separates a genuinely unusual segment signal from random variation caused by small denominators. This is directly aligned with the assignment requirement to use visual analytics for discovery rather than only descriptive charting.

6 Statistical validation

Visual analytics should lead discovery, but the strongest submission should not rely only on visual judgement. The validation layer is intentionally modest: it does not claim to replace actuarial pricing, but it checks whether the major visual differences remain statistically visible when assessed through standard non-parametric and frequency-model tools. This section uses statistical tests to check whether observed group differences are unlikely to be random noise.

6.1 Non-parametric comparison of policy-level loss ratio

Insurance loss ratio is extremely skewed, so the Kruskal-Wallis test is more appropriate than standard one-way ANOVA for policy-level loss-ratio comparisons.

Code 
kruskal_variables <- c(
  "policy_type", "bonus_score", "payment_frequency", "policy_status",
  "fuel_type", "municipality_type", "circulation_area", "business_type"
)

kruskal_results <- map_dfr(
  kruskal_variables,
  \(v) {
    formula <- as.formula(paste("loss_ratio_w99 ~", v))
    broom::tidy(kruskal.test(formula, data = portfolio))
  },
  .id = "variable_index"
) |>
  mutate(variable = kruskal_variables[as.integer(variable_index)]) |>
  select(variable, statistic, p.value, parameter, method)

kruskal_results |>
  mutate(
    statistic = number(statistic, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()

A significant result does not prove business causality, but it supports that the visual segment differences are not merely random sampling fluctuation.

6.2 Claim occurrence and categorical association

Code 
chi_square_results <- map_dfr(
  kruskal_variables,
  \(v) {
    tbl <- table(portfolio[[v]], portfolio$claim_flag)
    broom::tidy(chisq.test(tbl))
  },
  .id = "variable_index"
) |>
  mutate(variable = kruskal_variables[as.integer(variable_index)]) |>
  select(variable, statistic, p.value, parameter, method)

chi_square_results |>
  mutate(
    statistic = number(statistic, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()

The chi-square tests focus on claim occurrence, not incurred amount. This separates frequency risk from severity risk.

6.3 Logistic model for claim occurrence

Code 
claim_model_data <- portfolio |>
  filter(
    !is.na(driver_age),
    !is.na(vehicle_age),
    !is.na(vehicle_value),
    !is.na(total_exposure),
    total_exposure > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    claim_flag_int = as.integer(claim_flag),
    log_vehicle_value = log1p(vehicle_value)
  )

claim_model <- glm(
  claim_flag_int ~ policy_type + bonus_score + payment_frequency +
    policy_status + business_type + fuel_type + municipality_type +
    circulation_area + driver_age + vehicle_age + log_vehicle_value,
  data = claim_model_data,
  family = binomial()
)

claim_model_tidy <- broom::tidy(claim_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(log(estimate))))

claim_model_tidy |>
  slice_head(n = 25) |>
  mutate(
    estimate = number(estimate, accuracy = 0.01),
    conf.low = number(conf.low, accuracy = 0.01),
    conf.high = number(conf.high, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()

The logistic model is not used as a final pricing model. It is used as a validation layer to check whether variables that looked important visually still carry signal after adjusting for other observed characteristics.

Code 
claim_model_tidy |>
  filter(!str_detect(term, "vehicle_brand")) |>
  slice_head(n = 18) |>
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = my_blue) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted odds ratios for claim occurrence",
    subtitle = "Values above 1 indicate higher odds of at least one claim",
    x = "Odds ratio, log scale", y = NULL
  )

7 Synthesis of findings

The main findings are:

  1. Portfolio profitability weakened over time. The loss ratio increased by 9.0 percentage points from the first to the last year, while premium per exposure year changed by -9.2%. This is a pricing adequacy warning.
  2. Product type is a major source of profitability variation. COMP_N has the highest portfolio loss ratio at 93.9%, compared with 54.3% for TP.
  3. Cancellation is strongly associated with adverse experience. Cancelled policies show a portfolio loss ratio of 128.0%, compared with 64.4% for active policies. This should be investigated as an adverse-selection or post-claim cancellation signal.
  4. Payment frequency carries risk signal. S has the highest loss ratio, while Q has the highest claim frequency. This suggests payment structure may proxy behavioural or retention risk.
  5. Volatility is concentrated in the tail. Policy-level incurred losses and loss ratios are highly skewed; robust visual methods are necessary.

8 Recommendations

The analytical recommendations are:

  • Reprice or review high-loss product segments, especially policy types whose portfolio loss ratio approaches or exceeds the portfolio average by a large margin.
  • Separate frequency and severity in management dashboards. A high loss ratio may result from frequent small claims or rare severe claims; the remediation differs.
  • Monitor cancelled policies as an early-warning segment. The result is association, not causality, but the gap is too large to ignore.
  • Use bonus score and payment frequency jointly for underwriting review. These variables are operationally simple and visually meaningful.
  • Retain advanced distribution charts in the executive deck. Raincloud and ridgeline plots provide higher information density than basic boxplots while remaining interpretable.
  • Avoid treating this report as a pricing model. It is a visual analytics discovery report. Pricing would require actuarial modelling, temporal validation, exposure offsets, expense assumptions, and regulatory review.

9 Reproducibility notes

The report is fully reproducible in RStudio/Quarto if the two data files are placed in the data/ folder with these exact names:

  • Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv
  • Descriptive of variables.xlsx

The report intentionally keeps the full analytical workflow in executable R code chunks: package loading, data import, dictionary reconciliation, data cleaning, metric engineering, visual analytics, and statistical validation. No chart or table is manually typed from external software.

The Executive Summary is derived from this report. The two deliverables therefore share the same analytical spine: exposure-adjusted profitability, claim frequency, claim severity, loss-ratio volatility, segment comparison, distribution-shape diagnosis, interaction analysis, funnel-plot screening, statistical validation, and management recommendations.

safe_ratio <- function(numerator, denominator) {
  if_else(!is.na(denominator) & denominator > 0, numerator / denominator, NA_real_)

winsorise_upper <- function(x, p = 0.99) {
  cap <- quantile(x, probs = p, na.rm = TRUE)
  pmin(x, cap)
}

# Assignment purpose and analytical design {#assignment-purpose}
This report addresses the ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 requirement: use **visual analytics for data discovery** on a motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset. The analytical target is not only to describe the portfolio, but to identify where profitability and volatility differ across policy, customer, vehicle, and exposure characteristics.

The report uses the following logic:

1.  **Data audit and preparation**: verify row structure, missingness, duplicates, variable types, and construct actuarial performance metrics.
2.  **Univariate visual analytics**: examine the standalone distributions of premium, claims, incurred losses, exposure, loss ratio, and portfolio composition.
3.  **Bivariate visual analytics**: test how profitability and volatility differ by product, payment, claims-history, geography, vehicle, and policy-status segments.
4.  **Statistical validation**: support visual patterns with non-parametric tests and frequency modelling.
5.  **Business interpretation**: translate visual evidence into underwriting, pricing, and portfolio-management implications.

## Rubric alignment and deliverable logic {#rubric-alignment}
The technical report is written to support the Executive Summary rather than repeat it. The Executive Summary presents the decision story; this report documents the reproducible analytical evidence behind that story. The following table maps the report design to the assignment assessment logic.

| Assessment area | How this report addresses it |
|----|----|
| Data wrangling | Imports the raw semicolon-delimited portfolio file, reconciles the data dictionary, audits row structure, checks duplicates and missingness, converts categorical fields, and engineers exposure-adjusted performance metrics. |
| Visual analysis | Uses univariate and bivariate visual analytics to examine premium adequacy, claim frequency, severity, loss-ratio skewness, product effects, customer/vehicle/geography effects, and interaction effects. |
| Visual communication | Uses chart types selected for the structure of each question: bar charts for segment comparison, histograms for skewness, raincloud and ridgeline plots for distribution shape, funnel plots for exposure-adjusted outliers, and heatmaps for interactions. |
| Reproducibility | Shows the full R workflow: package loading, data import, cleaning, metric construction, plotting, summary tables, and statistical validation. |
| Additional visual methods | Adds raincloud plots, ridgeline plots, funnel-plot logic, and interaction heatmaps beyond simple descriptive charts. |

The methods are selected from the R for Visual Analytics materials only when they fit the data structure. Because insurance losses are highly right-skewed and zero-inflated, the report avoids relying only on means. It uses **weighted portfolio loss ratios**, **exposure-adjusted claim frequency**, **winsorised distributions**, **raincloud plots**, **ridgeline plots**, **heatmaps**, and **model-supported visual diagnostics**.

# Data import and dictionary reconciliation {#data-preparation}
```{r}
#| label: data-import

portfolio_raw <- readr::read_delim(
  "data/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv",
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  trim_ws = TRUE
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

dictionary_raw <- readxl::read_excel(
  "data/Descriptive of variables.xlsx",
  sheet = "Cartera"
) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

portfolio_raw |>
  glimpse()

dictionary_raw |>
  select(variables, description, group) |>
  filter(!is.na(variables)) |>
  gt::gt()
```

The CSV is semicolon-delimited. The data dictionary is used to verify variable meanings before metric engineering. The unit of observation is a policy-year record: the same `insured_id` may appear across multiple years.

```{r}
#| label: variable-check

dictionary_variables <- dictionary_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(variables)) |>
  pull(variables) |>
  janitor::make_clean_names()

column_check <- tibble(
  variable = union(names(portfolio_raw), dictionary_variables)
) |>
  mutate(
    in_dataset = variable %in% names(portfolio_raw),
    in_dictionary = variable %in% dictionary_variables
  )

column_check |>
  filter(!in_dataset | !in_dictionary) |>
  gt::gt()
```

A clean analysis should explicitly check whether dataset columns match the variable dictionary. Any mismatch would undermine reproducibility and interpretation.

# Data audit and preparation {#data-audit}
## Structural checks {#structural-checks}
```{r}
#| label: structural-checks

audit_summary <- tibble(
  metric = c(
    "Rows",
    "Columns",
    "Distinct insured_id",
    "Duplicate rows",
    "Years covered"
  ),
  value = c(
    nrow(portfolio_raw),
    ncol(portfolio_raw),
    n_distinct(portfolio_raw$insured_id),
    sum(duplicated(portfolio_raw)),
    paste(sort(unique(portfolio_raw$year)), collapse = ", ")
  )
)

audit_summary |>
  gt::gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: missingness-table

missingness <- portfolio_raw |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing_n") |>
  mutate(missing_pct = missing_n / nrow(portfolio_raw)) |>
  filter(missing_n > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))

missingness |>
  mutate(missing_pct = percent(missing_pct, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  gt::gt()
```

Only a small number of variables contain missing values. They are not dropped wholesale because insurance missingness may itself be informative. For visual analytics, missing categories are explicitly retained as `"Unknown"` where relevant.

## Metric engineering {#metric-engineering}
```{r}
#| label: metric-engineering

portfolio <- portfolio_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency,
        bonus_score, fuel_type, vehicle_brand, municipality_type, circulation_area),
      ~fct_na_value_to_level(as.factor(.x), level = "Unknown")
    ),
    claim_flag = total_claims > 0,
    loss_ratio = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_premium),
    profit = total_premium - total_incurred,
    profit_margin = safe_ratio(total_premium - total_incurred, total_premium),
    claim_frequency = safe_ratio(total_claims, total_exposure),
    premium_rate = safe_ratio(total_premium, total_exposure),
    incurred_rate = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_exposure),
    claim_severity = safe_ratio(total_incurred, total_claims),
    log_total_premium = log1p(total_premium),
    log_total_incurred = log1p(total_incurred),
    loss_ratio_w99 = winsorise_upper(loss_ratio, 0.99),
    incurred_w99 = winsorise_upper(total_incurred, 0.99),
    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf),
      labels = c("≤25", "26–35", "36–45", "46–55", "56–65", "66+")
    ),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 3, 7, 12, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("≤3", "4–7", "8–12", "13–20", "21+")
    ),
    vehicle_value_band = ntile(vehicle_value, 5),
    vehicle_value_band = factor(
      vehicle_value_band,
      levels = 1:5,
      labels = c("Lowest value", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Highest value")
    )
  )
```

The key profitability measure is the **portfolio loss ratio**:

\[ \text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Incurred Claims}}{\text{Total Premium}} \]

A value below 1 indicates underwriting profit before expenses; a value above 1 indicates that incurred claims exceed premium. For segment comparison, this report prioritises **portfolio-level weighted loss ratio** (`sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium)`) over simple average policy-level loss ratio, because large-premium policies should carry proportionate weight in portfolio profitability.

Volatility is represented by:

-   dispersion of policy-level loss ratio;
-   extreme incurred losses;
-   claim frequency per exposure year;
-   coefficient of variation of incurred cost;
-   outlier-sensitive segment loss ratios.

```{r}
#| label: derived-metric-summary

portfolio |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    total_exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    portfolio_loss_ratio = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_premium_rate = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_claim_severity = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(total_exposure, total_premium, total_incurred, total_claims,
             portfolio_loss_ratio, claim_frequency, avg_premium_rate, avg_claim_severity),
           ~round(.x, 3))
  ) |>
  gt::gt()
```

# Univariate visual analytics {#univariate-visual-analytics}
## Portfolio growth and exposure composition {#portfolio-overview}
```{r}
#| label: annual-summary

annual_summary <- portfolio |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    policies = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    portfolio_loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    premium_rate = premium / exposure,
    avg_severity = incurred / claims,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

annual_summary |>
  mutate(
    portfolio_loss_ratio = percent(portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1),
    claim_frequency = number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.001),
    premium_rate = dollar(premium_rate, prefix = "€", accuracy = 1),
    avg_severity = dollar(avg_severity, prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: annual-trend-plot
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8

p_annual_volume <- annual_summary |>
  pivot_longer(c(premium, incurred), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = value, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("premium" = my_light, "incurred" = my_blue)) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium and incurred losses both increased with portfolio growth",
    x = NULL, y = "Amount", fill = NULL
  )

p_annual_lr <- annual_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = portfolio_loss_ratio)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = my_blue) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = my_blue) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(annual_summary$year))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Portfolio loss ratio rose over time",
    x = NULL, y = "Portfolio loss ratio"
  )

p_annual_volume + p_annual_lr
```

The annual summary is essential because the assignment asks for discovery of profitability and volatility. The portfolio is not static: exposure, premium, incurred losses, and claim frequency all change over time.

## Distribution of premium, incurred losses, and loss ratio {#loss-distribution}
```{r}
#| label: univariate-distributions
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5

p_premium <- portfolio |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium distribution is right-skewed",
    x = "Total premium", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_incurred <- portfolio |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log1p(total_incurred))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Incurred loss is zero-heavy and extreme-tailed",
    x = "log(1 + total incurred)", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_lr <- portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio_w99)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = my_blue, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Winsorised loss ratio reveals core risk distribution",
    x = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile", y = "Policy-year count"
  )

p_premium + p_incurred + p_lr
```

The incurred-loss distribution is structurally different from the premium distribution. Premium is continuous and right-skewed, whereas incurred loss has many zero values and a heavy tail. This supports the use of robust visualisations and exposure-weighted metrics rather than raw averages alone.

## Claim count distribution {#claim-count-distribution}
```{r}
#| label: claim-count-distribution
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8

portfolio |>
  count(total_claims) |>
  mutate(
    claim_count_label = if_else(total_claims >= 5, "5+", as.character(total_claims))
  ) |>
  group_by(claim_count_label) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    claim_count_label = factor(claim_count_label, levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5+")),
    pct = n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_count_label, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_blue, colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Most policy-years have no claim, so claim occurrence must be modelled separately",
    x = "Total claims in policy-year", y = "Share of policy-years"
  )
```

This confirms a typical insurance portfolio pattern: most policies do not claim, while a minority drives incurred losses. That is why frequency and severity should be separated analytically.

## Product composition {#product-composition}
```{r}
#| label: product-composition
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

policy_composition <- portfolio |>
  group_by(policy_type) |>
  summarise(
    policies = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    policy_share = policies / sum(policies),
    exposure_share = exposure / sum(exposure),
    premium_share = premium / sum(premium),
    incurred_share = incurred / sum(incurred)
  )

policy_composition |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(policy_share, exposure_share, premium_share, incurred_share),
    names_to = "basis", values_to = "share"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    basis = recode(
      basis,
      policy_share = "Policy count",
      exposure_share = "Exposure",
      premium_share = "Premium",
      incurred_share = "Incurred"
    ),
    policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, share, .fun = max)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = share, fill = basis)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", colour = my_dark, linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D8E6F3", "#A9C7E8", "#6B9FD3", "#2F6DAE")) +
  labs(
    title = "Product mix is not the same as premium and incurred-loss mix",
    x = "Policy type", y = "Share of portfolio", fill = NULL
  )
```

Portfolio management should distinguish between count share, exposure share, premium share, and incurred share. A product with modest policy count can still dominate premium or loss contribution if coverage is broader or riskier.

## Ridgeline plot of premium rate by product {#premium-ridgeline}
```{r}
#| label: ridgeline-premium-rate
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(premium_rate), is.finite(premium_rate)) |>
  mutate(premium_rate_w99 = winsorise_upper(premium_rate, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = premium_rate_w99, y = fct_reorder(policy_type, premium_rate_w99, .fun = median))) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.4,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.3),
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline plot shows premium-rate separation across policy types",
    x = "Premium per exposure year, capped at 99th percentile",
    y = NULL
  )
```

This method is taken from the R4VA distribution chapter. It is suitable here because `policy_type` has multiple ordered groups and `premium_rate` is a continuous metric.

## Raincloud plot of loss ratio by product {#product-raincloud}
```{r}
#| label: raincloud-loss-ratio-policy
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

portfolio |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio_w99), is.finite(loss_ratio_w99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio_w99, .fun = median), y = loss_ratio_w99)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.18,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.35)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.16, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white", colour = my_dark) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.12,
    binwidth = 0.05,
    dotsize = 0.6,
    colour = my_blue
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud plot combines density, boxplot, and individual concentration",
    x = NULL, y = "Loss ratio capped at 99th percentile"
  )
```

The raincloud plot is stronger than a standard boxplot for this task because it exposes distribution shape and concentration while retaining median and IQR information. This directly supports the visual-discovery requirement.

## Distribution-shape add-on for adverse-experience policies {#distribution-shape}
The Executive Summary includes a distribution-shape add-on because the portfolio is zero-heavy: most policy-year records have no claims, while a small tail of adverse-experience policies drives volatility. This technical view deliberately filters to positive loss-ratio records and caps the displayed tail at the 95th percentile. The purpose is not to hide severe losses; the purpose is to make the shape among adverse records readable after the report has already established the scale of zero-claim dominance.

```{r}
#| label: distribution-shape-addon-positive-loss
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 5.5

positive_loss <- portfolio |>
  filter(
    !is.na(loss_ratio),
    is.finite(loss_ratio),
    loss_ratio > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(loss_ratio_positive_w95 = winsorise_upper(loss_ratio, 0.95))

p_positive_raincloud <- positive_loss |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = fct_reorder(policy_type, loss_ratio_positive_w95, .fun = median),
    y = loss_ratio_positive_w95
  )) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.6,
    justification = -0.16,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.40)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.14, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white", colour = my_dark) +
  ggdist::stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.08,
    binwidth = 0.04,
    dotsize = 0.45,
    colour = my_blue
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Positive-loss distribution by product",
    subtitle = "Zero-claim records excluded; loss ratio capped at 95th percentile for readability",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Positive loss ratio, capped"
  )

p_positive_ridgeline <- positive_loss |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = loss_ratio_positive_w95,
    y = fct_reorder(payment_frequency, loss_ratio_positive_w95, .fun = median)
  )) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.0,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    fill = colorspace::lighten(my_blue, 0.35),
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  ggridges::theme_ridges() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Positive-loss density by payment frequency",
    subtitle = "Compares adverse-experience distributions without the zero-claim mass",
    x = "Positive loss ratio, capped",
    y = NULL
  )

p_positive_raincloud + p_positive_ridgeline
```

The raincloud plot is appropriate because it combines distribution density, boxplot summary, and observation concentration in one view. The ridgeline plot is appropriate because it compares distribution shape across multiple ordered groups without forcing the reader to inspect separate charts. Together, these methods justify the executive conclusion that simple averages are unstable for this portfolio.

# Bivariate visual analytics {#bivariate-visual-analytics}
## Segment-performance function {#segment-performance-function}
```{r}
#| label: segment-function

segment_summary <- function(data, segment_var) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ segment_var }}) |>
    summarise(
      policies = n(),
      exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
      incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
      portfolio_loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
      claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
      premium_rate = premium / exposure,
      avg_severity = incurred / claims,
      mean_policy_loss_ratio = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_policy_loss_ratio = sd(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
      cv_incurred = sd(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(portfolio_loss_ratio))
}
```

For profitability, `portfolio_loss_ratio` is the primary measure. For volatility, this report uses claim frequency, average severity, policy-level loss-ratio dispersion, and incurred-loss coefficient of variation.

## Funnel plot for exposure-adjusted brand screening {#funnel-plot}

The Executive Summary includes a funnel plot because raw segment rankings can overreact to small-volume groups. In insurance portfolios, a vehicle brand with limited exposure can show an extreme claim frequency simply because the denominator is small. A funnel plot is therefore more defensible than a simple sorted bar chart when the analytical question is whether a segment is unusually high after accounting for exposure volume.

The funnel uses claim frequency as the outcome and exposure years as the denominator. The centre line is the overall portfolio claim frequency. The approximate 95% band widens at low exposure and narrows at high exposure, reflecting the higher random variation expected in small segments.

```{r}
#| label: funnel-plot-data
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

brand_funnel <- portfolio |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= quantile(exposure, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = fct_lump_n(vehicle_brand, n = 25, w = exposure)) |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(exposure),
    claims = sum(claims),
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(vehicle_brand != "Other")

overall_rate <- sum(portfolio$total_claims, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(portfolio$total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE)

funnel_curve <- tibble(
  exposure = seq(min(brand_funnel$exposure), max(brand_funnel$exposure), length.out = 200),
  expected = overall_rate,
  upper_95 = overall_rate + 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate / exposure),
  lower_95 = pmax(overall_rate - 1.96 * sqrt(overall_rate / exposure), 0)
)

flagged_brand <- brand_funnel |>
  mutate(distance = abs(claim_frequency - overall_rate)) |>
  slice_max(distance, n = 6, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = funnel_curve,
    aes(x = exposure, ymin = lower_95, ymax = upper_95),
    fill = "#D9E8F6",
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = funnel_curve,
    aes(x = exposure, y = expected),
    colour = my_blue,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = brand_funnel,
    aes(x = exposure, y = claim_frequency),
    colour = my_teal,
    size = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = flagged_brand,
    aes(x = exposure, y = claim_frequency, label = vehicle_brand),
    size = 3,
    vjust = -0.7,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Funnel plot: claim frequency by vehicle brand",
    subtitle = "Approximate 95% expected range after accounting for exposure size",
    x = "Exposure years",
    y = "Claims per exposure year"
  )
```

The funnel plot adds value because it separates a genuinely unusual segment signal from random variation caused by small denominators. This is directly aligned with the assignment requirement to use visual analytics for discovery rather than only descriptive charting.

# Statistical validation {#statistical-validation}
Visual analytics should lead discovery, but the strongest submission should not rely only on visual judgement. The validation layer is intentionally modest: it does not claim to replace actuarial pricing, but it checks whether the major visual differences remain statistically visible when assessed through standard non-parametric and frequency-model tools. This section uses statistical tests to check whether observed group differences are unlikely to be random noise.

## Non-parametric comparison of policy-level loss ratio {#nonparametric-validation}
Insurance loss ratio is extremely skewed, so the Kruskal-Wallis test is more appropriate than standard one-way ANOVA for policy-level loss-ratio comparisons.

```{r}
#| label: kruskal-tests

kruskal_variables <- c(
  "policy_type", "bonus_score", "payment_frequency", "policy_status",
  "fuel_type", "municipality_type", "circulation_area", "business_type"
)

kruskal_results <- map_dfr(
  kruskal_variables,
  \(v) {
    formula <- as.formula(paste("loss_ratio_w99 ~", v))
    broom::tidy(kruskal.test(formula, data = portfolio))
  },
  .id = "variable_index"
) |>
  mutate(variable = kruskal_variables[as.integer(variable_index)]) |>
  select(variable, statistic, p.value, parameter, method)

kruskal_results |>
  mutate(
    statistic = number(statistic, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()
```

A significant result does not prove business causality, but it supports that the visual segment differences are not merely random sampling fluctuation.

## Claim occurrence and categorical association {#claim-occurrence-validation}
```{r}
#| label: chi-square-tests

chi_square_results <- map_dfr(
  kruskal_variables,
  \(v) {
    tbl <- table(portfolio[[v]], portfolio$claim_flag)
    broom::tidy(chisq.test(tbl))
  },
  .id = "variable_index"
) |>
  mutate(variable = kruskal_variables[as.integer(variable_index)]) |>
  select(variable, statistic, p.value, parameter, method)

chi_square_results |>
  mutate(
    statistic = number(statistic, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()
```

The chi-square tests focus on claim occurrence, not incurred amount. This separates frequency risk from severity risk.

## Logistic model for claim occurrence {#logistic-model}
```{r}
#| label: logistic-model

claim_model_data <- portfolio |>
  filter(
    !is.na(driver_age),
    !is.na(vehicle_age),
    !is.na(vehicle_value),
    !is.na(total_exposure),
    total_exposure > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    claim_flag_int = as.integer(claim_flag),
    log_vehicle_value = log1p(vehicle_value)
  )

claim_model <- glm(
  claim_flag_int ~ policy_type + bonus_score + payment_frequency +
    policy_status + business_type + fuel_type + municipality_type +
    circulation_area + driver_age + vehicle_age + log_vehicle_value,
  data = claim_model_data,
  family = binomial()
)

claim_model_tidy <- broom::tidy(claim_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(log(estimate))))

claim_model_tidy |>
  slice_head(n = 25) |>
  mutate(
    estimate = number(estimate, accuracy = 0.01),
    conf.low = number(conf.low, accuracy = 0.01),
    conf.high = number(conf.high, accuracy = 0.01),
    p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value)
  ) |>
  gt::gt()
```

The logistic model is not used as a final pricing model. It is used as a validation layer to check whether variables that looked important visually still carry signal after adjusting for other observed characteristics.

```{r}
#| label: model-coef-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

claim_model_tidy |>
  filter(!str_detect(term, "vehicle_brand")) |>
  slice_head(n = 18) |>
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = my_blue) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted odds ratios for claim occurrence",
    subtitle = "Values above 1 indicate higher odds of at least one claim",
    x = "Odds ratio, log scale", y = NULL
  )
```

# Synthesis of findings {#synthesis}
```{r}
#| label: key-findings-objects
#| include: false

overall_lr <- sum(portfolio$total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(portfolio$total_premium, na.rm = TRUE)

worst_policy <- policy_type_summary |> slice_max(portfolio_loss_ratio, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
best_policy <- policy_type_summary |> slice_min(portfolio_loss_ratio, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

worst_payment <- payment_summary |> slice_max(portfolio_loss_ratio, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
highest_freq_payment <- payment_summary |> slice_max(claim_frequency, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

cancelled <- status_summary |> filter(policy_status == "C")
active <- status_summary |> filter(policy_status == "A")

annual_change <- annual_summary |>
  arrange(year) |>
  summarise(
    premium_rate_change = last(premium_rate) / first(premium_rate) - 1,
    loss_ratio_change_pp = (last(portfolio_loss_ratio) - first(portfolio_loss_ratio)) * 100,
    claim_frequency_change = last(claim_frequency) / first(claim_frequency) - 1
  )
```

The main findings are:

1.  **Portfolio profitability weakened over time.** The loss ratio increased by `r number(annual_change$loss_ratio_change_pp, accuracy = 0.1)` percentage points from the first to the last year, while premium per exposure year changed by `r percent(annual_change$premium_rate_change, accuracy = 0.1)`. This is a pricing adequacy warning.
2.  **Product type is a major source of profitability variation.** `r as.character(worst_policy$policy_type)` has the highest portfolio loss ratio at `r percent(worst_policy$portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)`, compared with `r percent(best_policy$portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)` for `r as.character(best_policy$policy_type)`.
3.  **Cancellation is strongly associated with adverse experience.** Cancelled policies show a portfolio loss ratio of `r percent(cancelled$portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)`, compared with `r percent(active$portfolio_loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)` for active policies. This should be investigated as an adverse-selection or post-claim cancellation signal.
4.  **Payment frequency carries risk signal.** `r as.character(worst_payment$payment_frequency)` has the highest loss ratio, while `r as.character(highest_freq_payment$payment_frequency)` has the highest claim frequency. This suggests payment structure may proxy behavioural or retention risk.
5.  **Volatility is concentrated in the tail.** Policy-level incurred losses and loss ratios are highly skewed; robust visual methods are necessary.

# Recommendations {#recommendations}
The analytical recommendations are:

-   **Reprice or review high-loss product segments**, especially policy types whose portfolio loss ratio approaches or exceeds the portfolio average by a large margin.
-   **Separate frequency and severity in management dashboards.** A high loss ratio may result from frequent small claims or rare severe claims; the remediation differs.
-   **Monitor cancelled policies as an early-warning segment.** The result is association, not causality, but the gap is too large to ignore.
-   **Use bonus score and payment frequency jointly for underwriting review.** These variables are operationally simple and visually meaningful.
-   **Retain advanced distribution charts in the executive deck.** Raincloud and ridgeline plots provide higher information density than basic boxplots while remaining interpretable.
-   **Avoid treating this report as a pricing model.** It is a visual analytics discovery report. Pricing would require actuarial modelling, temporal validation, exposure offsets, expense assumptions, and regulatory review.

# Reproducibility notes {#reproducibility-notes}
The report is fully reproducible in RStudio/Quarto if the two data files are placed in the `data/` folder with these exact names:

-   `Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv`
-   `Descriptive of variables.xlsx`

The report intentionally keeps the full analytical workflow in executable R code chunks: package loading, data import, dictionary reconciliation, data cleaning, metric engineering, visual analytics, and statistical validation. No chart or table is manually typed from external software.

The Executive Summary is derived from this report. The two deliverables therefore share the same analytical spine: exposure-adjusted profitability, claim frequency, claim severity, loss-ratio volatility, segment comparison, distribution-shape diagnosis, interaction analysis, funnel-plot screening, statistical validation, and management recommendations.
